    Marmots¶

    "The marmots remember the hill. The Yaoma remember the tide. Together they remember the island."

    A species of stout, burrowing beastfolk native to the two islands and sacred atoll of the Yaoma Tribe south of Zakarutia and east of Xobkua. Where the Yaoma are water-breathing merfolk who master tide and song, Marmots are hill-breathing burrowers who master stone and silence — the landward complement that lets a two-island sea people also be an island people.

    Asatru traders' pidgin famously confuses Yaoma and marmot (merfolk → marmot). Oceanist Yaoma find this hilarious and sometimes ceremonially call themselves "the marmots of the perfect ocean" — a joke that, in Marmot ears, is an honorific. The Marmots, for their part, call Yaoma tide-kin and themselves hill-kin without any confusion at all.

    Biology¶

    • Appearance: Stout, low-slung beastfolk 1.2–1.4m tall standing, 1.6–1.8m stretched in tunnel. Dense, water-shedding pelts in sandstone, basalt-gray, lichen-green, and cream. Broad heads with small rounded ears, prominent incisors (ever-growing — gnawing is hygiene), and short but powerful limbs ending in scooping claws. Torso is barrel-chested; fat reserves are tail- and hindquarter-stored. Unlike true rodents, Marmots are fully sapient, with human-proportioned hands (clawed but dextrous) and clear speech.
    • Build: Built for digging and hauling. A Marmot can shift its own bodyweight in packed island soil per minute. Their sense of vibration through stone is exquisite — they feel a footstep through 20m of basalt.
    • Lifespan: 45–60 years. Maturity at ~12. Elders are prized as living tunnel-maps.
    • Mage-cell expression: Very low to none. Marmots produce almost no mages; their few stone-sense adepts achieve through lifelong vibration-training what other species do with spells — detecting faults, finding water, predicting rockfall.
    • Diet: Omnivorous island generalists — tubers, cliff grasses, washed-up kelp, and the fat white grubs of the hill interior. They ferment kelp-tuber mash into a sour, strong hill brew that Yaoma profess to dislike and secretly trade pearls for.
    • Reproduction: Viviparous, 2–4 kits per litter. Kits remain in the burrow-hall for two years, learning tunnel-craft before surfacing.

    Society¶

    Marmots and Yaoma share the Yaoma Tribe polity as one nation, two ecologies:

    • Yaoma occupy water — pearl beds, song-corridors, reef gardens, the sacred governance atoll.
    • Marmots occupy hill — the inland spine of both islands, where they have dug labyrinthine but orderly burrow-towns into limestone and basalt.

    The arrangement is not conquest but symbiosis, codified as Oceanism's shore-purgatory: Yaoma live in the perfection-adjacent water and visit land; Marmots live in the draft-land and visit water only at the shoreline. Governance is shared through the Tide-Council on the atoll: seven elders chosen by Maenar/Amelia phases, of whom by ancient compact two seats are always Marmot — the Hill Voices — even though Marmots cannot stay submerged long.

    • Governance: Within burrow-towns, Marmots govern by hall-consensus: each family burrow-hall (10–25 Marmots) sends a "claw" to a hill moot. The moot does not vote — it digs — extending a ceremonial tunnel a handspan per meeting until consensus is reached; the length of tunnel records the difficulty of the decision. The Tide-Council's two Marmot seats are chosen by the hill moot on new-moon nights when tides are lowest and Yaoma can stand longest on the atoll.
    • Culture: Taciturn, engineering-minded, and deeply humorous in a dry, subterranean way. Their oral history is tunnel-mapped: each major event is encoded as a named bend, chamber, or fault-brace in the burrow. A Marmot elder reciting history literally walks you through it. They consider Yaoma song-scrolls beautiful but impractical — "you can't shelter kits in a song when it storms," a young Marmot will whisper, and an older one will cuff them gently and say, "but you remember the storm because someone sang it."
    • Architecture: Burrow-towns are marvels of drainage, ventilation, and tidal respect. The deepest galleries are tide-locked — sealed during high water, opened at low. Sleeping chambers are lined with woven kelp and hill-brew yeast that regulates humidity. Yaoma visiting inland are carried in slung water-hammocks; Marmots visiting the reef are fitted with wet kelp cloaks.
    • Economy: Marmots are the islands' landward economy: terracing, water-catchment, tuber/kelp farming, burrow maintenance, and above all stonework — the Yaoma have no hands suited for quarrying. Marmot-quarried basalt builds Yaoma atoll docks and tide walls; Yaoma-harvested pearls buy what Marmots lack. Deep-sea salvage recovered by Yaoma is hauled ashore and conserved by Marmots.

    Relations & Religion¶

    • Yaoma — tide-kin: Not allies — co-nationals. Intermarriage is biologically impossible, but adoption across species is common: a Yaoma clutch may be hill-nursed by a Marmot hall in a hot season; a Marmot kit may be tide-bathed by Yaoma song-keepers. The two peoples bury their dead together at the high-tide line — Marmots digging the grave above the line, Yaoma singing below it.
    • Religion: Oceanism — Marmots are Oceanists alongside the Yaoma, in the Marmot idiom. Where Yaoma Oceanism says ocean creatures are perfect, land creatures are drafts, Marmot Oceanism says we are the draft that learned to love its incompleteness — and therefore digs, terraces, and holds the hill so that the Yaoma's purgatory has a shore worth returning to. Oceanist pilgrims of both species perform the beaching vigil together: the Marmot shades the Yaoma's gills with wet kelp while the Yaoma sings.
    • Zakarutia & Glub Kingdom: Marmots have no independent foreign policy; as part of the Yaoma Tribe they are represented by the Tide-Council. Zakarutian traders find Marmot stonework excellent; Glub slimes unsettle Yaoma but intrigue Marmots, who see in Slime confluence a burrow-like merging.
    • Demon Continent mainland: Marmot hill brew and Yaoma pearls travel north together as a paired export — "tide and hill" in one cargo.

    Role in the Yaoma Tribe¶

    Without Marmots, the Yaoma would be a tribe of brilliant singers and divers with nowhere dry to incubate eggs safely through a storm, nowhere to store salvage, and no one to quarry the atoll's governance stones. Without Yaoma, Marmots would be an isolated hill folk with no pearl wealth, no deep-water food, and no song to remember their tunnels by. Oceanism's core image — shoreline as purgatory between perfection and draft — is built on this interdependence.

    Asatru mainland reports once classified the islands as "Yaoma Tribe (mermaid-like, two islands)" and missed the Marmots entirely because censustakers stayed on the beach. The Tide-Council corrected the record by sending a Marmot delegation to waddle up the beach, dig a perfect, dry-footed negotiation pit on the sand, and offer hill brew inside it. The report was amended.
